subject: Vocabulary
topic: Collocations — Verb + Noun, Adjective + Noun Fixed Pairs for SSC CGL (W13 B1)

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: The mayor will ___ a press conference tomorrow to address the water crisis.
questions.explanation: C is correct. The correct collocation is HOLD a press conference / HOLD a meeting / HOLD an event. You HOLD (not make/do/give) scheduled formal events. Similarly: hold a rally, hold an election, hold a seminar. Trap: 'give a press conference' — while 'give a speech/presentation' is valid, 'give a press conference' is non-standard; the fixed collocation is 'hold'. 'Make a press conference' = incorrect. 'Do a press conference' = informal and non-standard.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: The new tax regulation will ___ effect from the first of April.
questions.explanation: B is correct. TAKE EFFECT = to begin to operate or be implemented (the law/policy becomes active). Fixed collocation: a law/rule/medicine 'takes effect'. Other TAKE collocations: take action, take responsibility, take a risk, take notice, take turns. Trap: 'make effect' = incorrect; 'bring effect' = non-standard (the phrase is 'bring into effect' which is acceptable, but not 'bring effect' alone); 'do effect' = completely wrong.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: The new research has ___ light on the causes of the mysterious ancient extinction.
questions.explanation: B is correct. SHED LIGHT ON = to make something clearer; to illuminate an issue. This is the standard collocation in formal written English (essays, articles, editorials). 'Cast light on' is also used but less formal. 'Throw light on' is another variant. In SSC English, the standard answer expected is SHED. Careful: all three (shed, throw, cast) appear in different dictionaries as acceptable, but SSC typically marks SHED as the primary collocation. Trap: 'given light on' = completely incorrect (you don't 'give light on' a problem).

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: The government must ___ awareness about the dangers of antibiotic resistance among the general public.
questions.explanation: C is correct. RAISE AWARENESS = to increase public consciousness of an issue. RAISE is transitive — it takes an object. 'Raise' collocations: raise awareness, raise funds, raise a question, raise an objection, raise the bar, raise eyebrows. Trap: 'rise' = intransitive (prices rise, standards rise — no object). 'Arise' = to appear or come into existence (a problem arises — intransitive). 'Rouse' = to awaken or provoke emotion (rouse a crowd, rouse suspicion) — while similar, 'rouse awareness' is non-standard. Only RAISE AWARENESS is the fixed collocation.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: Despite the setbacks, the team managed to ___ a victory against all odds.
questions.explanation: C is correct. SNATCH A VICTORY = to unexpectedly win at the last moment, especially when winning seems unlikely. This collocation perfectly captures 'against all odds' (unexpected outcome). Other uses: 'snatch defeat from the jaws of victory' (famous idiom). Trap: 'make a victory' = non-standard; 'do a victory' = incorrect; 'take a victory' = 'take a win' is informal sports usage but 'take a victory' is less standard than 'snatch a victory' when the context specifies 'against all odds'.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: The journalist was known for ___ a grudge against any politician who refused to speak to her.
questions.explanation: C is correct. HOLD A GRUDGE = to continue to feel resentment or anger towards someone; the fixed collocation. 'Hold a grudge' is the dominant form in written English (formal/journalistic). Note: 'bear a grudge' is also correct and used in formal English ('bear no grudge'). 'Keep a grudge' = non-standard. 'Carry a grudge' = occasionally used but less standard than 'hold'. In SSC, 'HOLD a grudge' is the preferred answer. Trap: 'bearing a grudge' is also acceptable but when given as an option alongside 'holding', SSC typically marks 'holding' as the primary collocation.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: The new infrastructure investment is expected to ___ rise to thousands of jobs in rural areas.
questions.explanation: B is correct. GIVE RISE TO = to cause something to happen; to be the origin or source of something. Fixed phrase: 'give rise to + noun'. Examples: 'The decision gave rise to widespread protests.' 'Warm temperatures give rise to more frequent storms.' Trap: 'take rise to' = incorrect (not a standard phrase); 'make rise to' = incorrect; 'bring rise to' = non-standard. 'Bring about' is valid but 'bring rise to' is not. Only GIVE RISE TO is the fixed expression.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: The CEO's announcement ___ a wave of panic among investors, leading to a sharp drop in share prices.
questions.explanation: D is correct. TRIGGER A WAVE OF PANIC = to set off or cause a sudden surge of fear. 'Trigger' collocates naturally with strong, sudden reactions: trigger a reaction, trigger panic, trigger a response, trigger an alarm. The metaphor of 'wave' (a wave of panic, a wave of protests) pairs with 'triggered' because waves follow from a sudden cause. Trap: 'created panic' = acceptable in general use but 'created a wave of panic' is less idiomatic than 'triggered'; 'made a wave' = incorrect; 'did panic' = completely wrong.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: The defence minister assured that the government would ___ no stone unturned to bring the perpetrators to justice.
questions.explanation: B is correct. LEAVE NO STONE UNTURNED = to try every possible means; to make every effort. This is a fixed idiom that must be used in its EXACT form. 'Leave no stone unturned' = standard expression meaning to do everything possible. The verb is ALWAYS 'leave' in this idiom — no substitution is allowed. Trap: 'keep no stone unturned' = grammatically sounds similar but is NOT the correct idiom; the correct form is 'leave'. This tests whether students know the idiom's exact wording, which is a common SSC distinction test.

questions.stem: Choose the correct collocation: The investigative report ___ serious doubts about the integrity of the procurement process.
questions.explanation: B is correct. RAISE DOUBTS = to cause someone to have doubts; to introduce reasons for scepticism. RAISE collocates with: raise doubts, raise concerns, raise questions, raise objections, raise eyebrows, raise suspicion. These are all situations where an issue is being put forward (raised) for consideration. Trap: 'create doubts' = while 'create' can introduce things, 'raise doubts' is the established collocation in formal/journalistic English; 'make doubts' = incorrect; 'brought doubts' = 'bring' would need 'brought up doubts' or 'brought doubts to light' but not 'brought doubts' alone.
